boards.title: What a line is

floors.content:
Look at the image. What do you see?

A pencil dragged across paper. The horizon where sea meets sky. A thread pulled tight between two fingers. A crack in dry earth. A beam of light in a dark room.

Each of these is a line. Not the same kind of line — one is drawn, one is seen, one is held — but they all share something. They are all straight. They all have no thickness. A thread has width if you look close enough, but the idea of a line does not.

Strip away the pencil lead, the water, the fibre. What is left?

A line is the shortest path between two points. If you put two dots on a page, there is exactly one straight path that joins them without waste — no curve, no wobble, no extra distance. That path is a line.

It has no thickness. You cannot measure how wide a line is, because width belongs to the physical thing that draws it, not to the line itself. A line is one-dimensional: it has length and nothing else.

Now take away the two points.

A geometric line does not stop. It extends forever in both directions — no start, no end. This is the Euclidean line, the one mathematicians mean when they say "line" without qualification.

A segment is the piece of a line between two endpoints — what you actually draw. A ray starts at a point and goes forever in one direction — like light from a bulb. But a line goes forever both ways. It is the pure idea, and the other two borrow from it.

This distinction — line vs segment vs ray — will matter every time we talk about direction, distance, and position from here on.

The line should be slightly imperfect — not ruler-straight — to feel human and hand-drawn. No other elements. Clean, minimal, editorial style.
